newsitem.title: USA: Utility tax plan would up Fla. school bonding.
newsitem.headline: Utility tax plan would up Fla. school bonding.

text.p: A proposal to be submitted to the Florida Governor's Committee on Education would expand the state's gross receipts tax on utilities to increase the state's school bond capacity.

The proposal was approved Tuesday by the commission's school funding committee and will go before the full commission on Thursday. If approved there, it would then go before the Legislature during the annual session that begins next week.
Florida has gained 58,000 students a year over the last nine years, and will need 251 new schools by the 2001 to keep up with enrollment, the commission said.

Three-fourths of the money Florida uses to build schools comes from local property taxes. The rest comes from the 2.5 percent utilities gross receipts tax on telephones, electricity and gas services, which is leveraged via Florida Board of Education bonds.
The tax raises enough money to back about $600 million of new bonds annually. But as new bonds are issued and debt service rises, the bond capacity will shrink to about $545 million in 2001.
The committee's proposal would apply the gross receipts tax to cable television, garbage collection and water and sewer services, which are now exempt.
It would be phased in over five years, adding 0.5 percent to the tax rate each year until the rate reaches the 2.5 percent already applied to the other utilities.
The plan would add about $2 to consumers' monthly utility bills, and raise enough money to issue another $1 billion of school bonds over the next five years, the commission said.

The education commission was appointed by Democratic Gov. Lawton Chiles and was expected to meet with resistance in the Republican-controlled legislature, whose leaders have pledged not to raise taxes.
